newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish bombers may have had fake passes.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish bombers may have had fake passes.

text.p: The British army on Tuesday ordered an urgent security review after guerrillas penetrated its Northern Ireland headquarters with an audacious double car bomb attack.

Forged identity documents and slack security may have been vital factors in helping Republican extremists slip through the heavily-fortified headquarters at Lisburn, near Belfast, on Monday and detonate up to 1000 lb (450 kg) of explosives.

Britain said the Irish Republican Army (IRA), which ended a 17-month truce in February, was the prime suspect. But a maverick group, the Irish Continuity Army Council, claimed the attack in an telephone call to Ireland's RTE broadcasting network.
Security sources said the bombers seemed to have a thorough knowledge of the base lay-out for the meticulously-planned operation.
The blasts, 20 minutes apart, injured 31 people and sent shockwaves through the quiet town of Lisburn where many had regarded the army base as virtually impenetrable.
"There is no such thing...as absolute security," Britain's Northern Ireland security Sir Patrick Mayhew told reporters.
"Of course there will be an inquiry, it is going on now under the direction of the RUC (police) into how this breach of security happened."

Security is normally rigorous for ingoing and outgoing traffic at the sprawling base, home to hundreds of army families as well as 2,000 military and civilian staff steering Britain's anti-guerrilla strategies.
The second bomb, outside a medical centre, seemed designed to catch people being rushed there after the first explosion.
Civilians and journalists who have visited the complex say names of visitors are registered in advance at a reception check-in area by the staff on the base they are due to visit.
Vehicle are screened by under-car mirrors to guard against explosives. Staff require passes to enter the precincts.
Military experts said the bombers may have tampered with a security pass, either completely falsifying it or using a fake photograph, and posed as bona fide visitors or staff.
"How that person got out -- that remains a mystery," Michael Dewar, a former deputy director of the International Institute for Strategic Studies told Reuters.

"Another possibility is that they used an innocent worker's car, who was unaware of the load he was taking in and that it was detonated by radio from outside the perimeter...But then we exploding outside the medical centre."
Gary Ellis, deputy editor of the Lisburn Star newspaper, said there may have been lax checking of personnel or the bombers had access to people working there and forged their passes.
The investigators would have to probe whether there had been "dummy runs", he said. The operation had been well planned and looked as if it had been "tried and tested".
Dewar said that if the IRA was resuming offensive action in the province, it was because of British security forces' successes against the guerrillas' mainland bombing campaign.
"In a sense it (the attack) is a stunning success from the terrorist perspective but it is also a result of their failure to achieve success on the mainland," Dewar said.
